opus-5.5.text:
I don't think there will be a single moment where everyone wakes up and says, "Okay, today AGI arrived." It's more like a continuous process. If you look back, every time models gained a new capability, like writing fluent text, coding, or doing multi-step reasoning, people first said "this is amazing," and a few months later it became the baseline. The goalposts keep moving, and I think that's natural, because our definition of intelligence is itself shaped by what machines can't yet do.

So I tend to think less about a declaration and more about measurable thresholds. One way I look at it is: what fraction of economically valuable work, or of meaningful cognitive tasks, can the system do end to end, reliably, without a human in the loop? That number rises gradually. At some point it crosses fifty percent, then eighty, and somewhere along that curve people will retroactively say, "That was probably when it happened." But in the moment it won't feel like a clean line.

There's also a deeper point. AGI isn't really a fixed endpoint. Even if a model can do everything a strong human expert can do, the more interesting question is whether it can keep improving itself, explore new knowledge, and solve problems humans haven't solved. In that sense AGI is less a destination and more a starting point for something else. From the perspective of building these systems, it's more useful to focus on the next concrete capability gap, like long-horizon agentic tasks, or learning efficiently from limited data, than to debate when to put up a banner.

So my honest answer: the declaration matters much less than the trajectory. Historians might pick a date later, but for those of us doing the work, it will feel like one step after another.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI will not have a clean, universally recognized moment, but it does not compare pinpointing that moment with identifying the achievement of a moon landing.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think there will be a single moment where someone stands up and says, "Today, AGI is achieved." That's a bit like asking when the internet "arrived." It arrived gradually, and then one day you realized you couldn't live without it.

The way I think about it, AGI is less a threshold and more a process. If you look at the past few years, every time a model crossed what people used to call the AGI bar, the bar moved. GPT-3 could write coherent paragraphs, and people said that's not real understanding. Then models passed professional exams, and people said that's just memorization. Then they started writing working code and doing multi-step reasoning, and the goalposts shifted again. So the question of "declaring a moment" assumes there's a stable definition, and in practice there isn't.

What I find more useful is to think in terms of capabilities and economic impact. Can the system learn a new task from a small amount of experience, the way a competent human would? Can it operate autonomously over long horizons, make decisions, correct its own mistakes? Can it do a meaningful fraction of the cognitive work that people are paid to do today? When you frame it that way, you start to see AGI not as a point but as a curve. We're somewhere on that curve, and the slope is steep.

There's also a scaling perspective here. Intelligence, in these systems, grows fairly smoothly with compute, data, and better algorithms. Smooth curves don't have natural "moments." What creates the sense of a moment is when a smooth capability gain crosses a discrete threshold in the real world, like being good enough to replace a specific job, or good enough that people trust it with real decisions. Those thresholds are social and economic, not technical.

So if you force me to answer, I'd say the declaration will come retrospectively. Ten years from now, people will look back and argue about which year it happened, the same way historians argue about when the industrial revolution started. And honestly, I think that's fine. What matters isn't the label. What matters is whether we're building systems that keep getting more useful, more reliable, and more aligned with what people actually need. If we do that well, the question of when exactly we "achieved" AGI becomes almost a footnote.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI may arrive gradually and compares it to the internet’s arrival, but it does not compare pinpointing AGI to pinpointing a moon landing.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s difficult to identify a single moment, because it depends on what we mean by AGI. If we define it through a particular benchmark, we might reach that benchmark without having a system that can reliably handle the broad range of tasks we care about.

I would think about it more as a process. Can the system learn new things, solve unfamiliar problems, and carry out complex tasks with less human guidance? And how consistently can it do those things? We may see those capabilities emerge at different times.

So I’m less focused on a declaration that AGI has arrived. I think the more meaningful question is what the system can actually do, where it still fails, and whether those limitations are becoming smaller.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AGI is difficult to identify at a single moment, but does not compare this difficulty with pinpointing a moon landing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s hard to identify a single moment, because AGI itself isn’t a very precise definition. People have different expectations: is it doing most economically valuable work, making scientific discoveries, or learning new tasks as effectively as a human? Depending on the definition, you’ll get a different answer.

I would focus more on the capabilities we can actually demonstrate. Can the system handle unfamiliar problems? Can it work reliably over a long period without someone constantly correcting it? Can it produce new knowledge? Those are more useful questions than whether we should announce that we’ve crossed a particular line.

And I suspect the transition will look uneven. A system might be much better than humans in some areas and still make surprisingly basic mistakes in others. So there may be a period when some people say AGI has arrived and others disagree. The label matters less than understanding what the system can do and where its limitations are.

r001.rationale: The response says identifying a single AGI moment is hard because AGI is imprecisely defined and capabilities may develop unevenly. It does not compare this difficulty with pinpointing the achievement of a moon landing.
